_meta: A small clean dataset and a set of outlier magnitudes, used to show the breakdown point of the mean versus the median -- how many corrupted data points it takes to move each summary arbitrarily far. This is about contamination (a data-entry typo, a sensor glitch, a parsing error that reads a field wrong), not about a genuinely skewed distribution. The mean has a breakdown point of zero: a single bad value, pushed large enough, drags the mean arbitrarily far, because the mean is a sum divided by n and one enormous term dominates the sum. The median has a breakdown point of one half: it is the middle order statistic, so a corrupted value only changes which value sits in the middle, and to push the median outside the range of the clean data you must corrupt more than half the points. The consequence is that on any dataset that might contain even one error -- which is almost every real dataset -- the mean is not a trustworthy summary, and a robust estimator (the median, or a trimmed mean) is. This is distinct from the mean-versus-median-on-skewed-data question (a companion module): there the tail is real and the mean is the right estimator for a total; here the outlier is an error and the mean is simply wrong. clean is the uncontaminated data; outlier_sizes are magnitudes to inject as a single contaminating point. These are the fixture; the mean and median of the clean data, of the data with one outlier of each size, and under corrupting an increasing number of points, are computed.
